title: ISO 9001 vs ISO 13485: what is the difference for quality management and training?
description: ISO 9001 is the general quality management standard; ISO 13485 is the medical device standard written for regulators. How scope and competence differ.
shortAnswer: ISO 9001 is the general international standard for quality management systems, usable by any organization; its sixth edition, ISO 9001:2026, was published on September 16, 2026. ISO 13485:2016 is a separate standard for organizations involved in the design, production, installation and servicing of medical devices, written for regulatory purposes. Both require competent personnel, but ISO 13485 is the one regulators use: the US FDA has incorporated it by reference into its Quality Management System Regulation since February 2, 2026.
keyTakeaways: ISO 9001 applies to any organization and sector; ISO 13485 is specific to medical devices and related services and is titled "Requirements for regulatory purposes".
ISO 13485 began in 1996 as particular requirements for applying ISO 9001 to medical devices and has since evolved into a stand alone standard, according to the FDA.
Competence sits in clause 7.2 of ISO 9001 and clause 6.2 of ISO 13485; ISO 9001:2026 also adds awareness of quality culture and ethical behavior in clause 7.3.
Since February 2, 2026, FDA's QMSR (21 CFR Part 820) requires device manufacturers to comply with ISO 13485:2016, but FDA does not require or issue ISO 13485 certificates.
ISO 9001 certified organizations have three years to transition to the 2026 edition; ISO 13485 remains at its 2016 edition.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between ISO 9001 and ISO 13485?

blocks.text: The core difference is purpose. ISO 9001 is a general quality management standard focused on consistently meeting customer and applicable requirements and on improvement. ISO 13485 is written so that medical device organizations can demonstrate a quality management system that meets regulatory requirements, which is why regulators reference it directly.

[ISO 9001:2026](https://www.iso.org/standard/9001), the sixth edition, was published on September 16, 2026 and replaces ISO 9001:2015. ISO says the clause structure is unchanged and that the [main changes](https://www.iso.org/quality-management/iso-9001-2026) include greater emphasis on quality culture and ethical behavior, a clearer distinction between risks and opportunities, and new awareness requirements in clause 7.3. Detail is on [ISO 9001 competence requirements](/regulations/iso-9001-competence-requirements).

[ISO 13485:2016](https://www.iso.org/iso-13485-medical-devices.html), Medical devices: Quality management systems: Requirements for regulatory purposes, is designed for organizations involved in the design, production, installation and servicing of medical devices and related services. ISO says certification is not a requirement of the standard, but third party certification can demonstrate to regulators that the requirements have been met.

blocks.text: The FDA's final rule explains the relationship: ISO first issued ISO 13485 in 1996 as a set of particular requirements for applying ISO 9001 to medical devices, to be used in conjunction with ISO 9001, and over time it "has evolved into a stand-alone standard" ([89 FR 7496](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2024/02/02/2024-01709.txt)).

sections.heading: How do their competence and training expectations differ?

blocks.text: Both require organizations to make people competent for work that affects quality and to keep evidence. The difference is the setting: ISO 13485 competence evidence is inspected by device regulators, so records must survive regulatory as well as certification scrutiny.

ISO 9001 clause 7.2 requires the organization to determine necessary competence, ensure people are competent through education, training or experience, take action to close gaps and evaluate whether it worked, and retain evidence. The 2026 edition adds awareness of quality culture and ethical behavior in clause 7.3, which means awareness content needs updating during transition.

For ISO 13485, the FDA's final rule states that Clause 6.2 requires individuals doing work that impacts quality to be competent on the basis of appropriate education, training, skills and expertise, covering internal and external personnel, full and part time staff, contractors and consultants, and that all education, training, skills and experience need to be carefully recorded. Under the [QMSR](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/postmarket-requirements-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr), failure to comply renders a device adulterated. Detail is on [FDA QMSR training requirements](/regulations/fda-qmsr-training-requirements).

sections.heading: Which standard applies to your organization?

blocks.text: If the organization makes, services or supplies medical devices or related services, ISO 13485 is the relevant standard, and for US device manufacturers it is effectively mandatory through the QMSR. Everyone else uses ISO 9001 if they want a certifiable quality management system.

items: **Medical device manufacturers selling in the US:** comply with ISO 13485:2016 as incorporated in 21 CFR Part 820, whether or not certified.
**Device suppliers and service providers:** customers often expect ISO 13485; check contracts and the regulatory requirements of the markets you supply.
**General manufacturers and service firms:** ISO 9001, with transition to the 2026 edition planned within the three year window.

**Organizations with both device and non device business:** many run both standards over one system; map each competence requirement to both clauses and keep one record set. A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) is the usual tool.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps role competencies to ISO 9001 clause 7.2, ISO 13485 clause 6.2 and the QMSR in a single framework, with provenance to each source. The ISO 9001:2026 awareness changes can then be applied once and traced to every affected module, and the same competence records serve certification audits and FDA inspections.

faqs.q: Does ISO 13485 certification include ISO 9001 certification?
faqs.a: No. They are separate standards with separate certificates. ISO 13485 shares origins and many concepts with ISO 9001 but is now a stand alone standard. Organizations that want both certificates are assessed against both, often in combined audits.

faqs.q: Does FDA accept an ISO 13485 certificate instead of inspection?
faqs.a: No. FDA's QMSR FAQ states that FDA will not require or issue ISO 13485 certificates and that a certificate does not exempt a manufacturer from FDA inspection. Compliance with the incorporated standard is assessed by FDA directly.

faqs.q: Will ISO 13485 be updated to match ISO 9001:2026?
faqs.a: ISO 13485:2016 remains the current edition on ISO's site as at November 2026, and the FDA's QMSR incorporates the 2016 edition specifically. Any future revision would need its own transition, so monitor ISO and FDA announcements rather than assume alignment with ISO 9001:2026.

faqs.q: Do contractors and consultants need competence records under ISO 13485?
faqs.a: Yes, according to the FDA's reading of Clause 6.2 in the QMSR final rule, which lists internal and external personnel, full and part time staff, contractors and consultants as examples of people whose competence must be ensured and recorded when their work affects quality.
